1. For the clinic register, Sxy = 928.6, Sxx = 6190.8, x̄ = 24.35 months and ȳ = 12.15 kg. Compute b₁ and b₀. Then find the fitted weight and the residual for a 30-month-old child who weighs 12.0 kg.

b₁ = Sxy ÷ Sxx = 928.6 ÷ 6190.8 = 0.150 kg per month. b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄ = 12.15 − 0.150 × 24.35 = 12.15 − 3.65 = 8.50 kg. Fitted weight at 30 months: 8.50 + 0.150 × 30 = 8.50 + 4.50 = 13.00 kg. Residual = observed − fitted = 12.0 − 13.0 = −1.0 kg: this child is 1 kg lighter than the model predicts for her age.

2. Children in a school are weighed, and the 20 thinnest are enrolled in a feeding programme. Three months later their mean BMI z-score has risen. Name one reason, other than the programme, why their mean would rise, and one design feature that would remove it.

Regression to the mean: the 20 were selected because their first measurement was extreme, and part of that extremeness was measurement error and short-term fluctuation (a recent illness, a measurement slip), which is not repeated at the second weighing. Their mean would move towards the population mean even with no programme. (Normal growth and seasonal change are further reasons.) A randomised control group chosen in the same way (thinnest children, half not fed) regresses by the same amount, so the programme’s effect is the difference between groups. Selecting on the mean of two baseline measurements also reduces the problem.

3. Two variables have r = 0.5. A person is 2 SD above the mean of x. How many SDs above the mean of y is the predicted value?

In SD units the prediction is r times the predictor: (ŷ − ȳ)/s_y = r × (x − x̄)/s_x = 0.5 × 2 = 1.0 SD above the mean of y.

1. A colleague adds a fourth predictor to a model and R² rises from 0.41 to 0.43. They conclude the new predictor is clinically important. What is the flaw, and what should they check instead?

Adding any predictor, even random numbers, can only lower SSE, so R² can only rise; the rise says nothing about importance. They should check adjusted R² (which rises only if the new predictor’s |t| exceeds 1, itself a low bar), and, above all, the new predictor’s coefficient and 95% CI in clinical units: is the size of the association compatible with the data large enough to matter?

2. Explain, using the error term, why a fitted line almost never passes through every data point, even when the model is a good one.

The model is Y = β₀ + β₁X + ε. The error term ε holds everything that affects the outcome besides X: other causes, individual variation and measurement error. The line describes the average outcome at each x; individuals scatter around it by their own ε. A good model gets the average right; it was never meant to predict every individual exactly.

3. A regression of haemoglobin (g/dL) on weeks of iron supplementation in 27 women gives b₁ = 0.12 g/dL per week, s = 0.9 g/dL and Sxx = 900 weeks². Compute SE(b₁), the t statistic and the 95% CI for β₁ (t₂₅ = 2.060). Is the result compatible with no linear association?

SE(b₁) = s ÷ √Sxx = 0.9 ÷ 30 = 0.03 g/dL per week. t = 0.12 ÷ 0.03 = 4.0 on 27 − 2 = 25 df. 95% CI = 0.12 ± 2.060 × 0.03 = 0.12 ± 0.062 = 0.058 to 0.182 g/dL per week. The interval excludes zero (p < 0.001, since |t| = 4.0 is far beyond 2.06), so the data are not compatible with a flat line; they are compatible with gains from about 0.06 to 0.18 g/dL per week.

1. A residual-vs-fitted plot shows residuals fanning out into a cone as fitted values increase. Which assumption is violated, and what does it threaten: the coefficient, or something else?

Equal variance (homoscedasticity) is violated: heteroscedasticity. It threatens the standard errors, and so the CIs and p-values built from them. The coefficient itself can remain a reasonable estimate; its reported precision is what becomes unreliable.

2. Why does violating independence raise the risk of a false-positive result, rather than just making the estimate less precise?

Correlated observations (children in the same village, repeated visits by one child) carry less information than the same number of independent ones. The model treats each as fresh information, so it computes an SE that is too small. A too-small SE gives too-narrow CIs and too-small p-values, so a null association is declared significant more often than 5% of the time: the Type I error rate rises.

3. The clinic regression (SE of the slope 0.011 kg per month) is refitted on children who were in fact sampled in village clusters, with a design effect of 2.44 for the slope. Roughly what is the correct SE, and what happens to the width of the 95% CI?

DEFF multiplies the variance (recall §6.2.6), so the SE is multiplied by √DEFF = √2.44 = 1.56. Correct SE ≈ 0.011 × 1.56 = 0.017 kg per month. The 95% CI is about 1.56 times as wide: roughly 0.150 ± 2 × 0.017 = 0.116 to 0.184 kg per month instead of 0.129 to 0.171.

1. Household wealth and household electricity access are strongly correlated. In a model containing both, each has a wide CI and neither is significant, though R² is high. What is the likely explanation, and how would you confirm it?

Multicollinearity. The two predictors share most of their variation, so the model cannot separate their individual contributions: each coefficient’s SE is inflated, though together they explain the outcome well (hence the high R²). Confirm with the variance inflation factor (VIF): large VIFs for both, and a large R²ⱼ when one is regressed on the other. A joint F-test of the two (the nested-model F-test taught later, in §12.4.5) would be significant even though neither t-test is.

2. A crude regression coefficient for a drug’s effect is 0.90, and the coefficient adjusted for age is 0.35. What does this comparison show, and what does it not show?

It shows that age accounts for a large part of the crude association, which is consistent with age confounding the drug–outcome relationship (for example, if older patients both received the drug more often and had higher outcome values). It does not by itself prove confounding: the shift could partly reflect chance or model specification, and whether age is a confounder (associated with drug use, affecting the outcome, not on the causal path) must be argued from subject-matter knowledge before fitting. The adjusted 0.35 also remains open to confounding by unmeasured variables.

3. In a model with an interaction, b₁ (supplement) = 0.30 kg and b₃ (supplement × malnourished) = 0.50 kg. What is the supplement’s estimated effect in malnourished children? Separately: regressing one predictor on the others gives R²ⱼ = 0.75. What is its VIF, and by what factor is its SE inflated?

Effect in malnourished children = b₁ + b₃ = 0.30 + 0.50 = 0.80 kg (0.30 kg applies only to well-nourished children, the reference group). VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.75) = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4. The variance of that coefficient is 4 times what it would be without the correlation, so the SE is √4 = 2 times larger.

1. A study reports “children with maternal BMI ≥ 25 had 0.4 kg higher birthweight (p = 0.04)”, after the authors tried cut-offs of 22, 23, 24, 25 and 26. Give two reasons this analysis is weak, and say how you would reanalyse it.

  1. Dichotomising a continuous predictor discards information and power, and treats a mother at BMI 25.1 like one at 35. (ii) The cut-off was chosen as the most significant of five tries, a multiple-comparisons problem that biases the estimate away from zero and inflates the false-positive rate; p = 0.04 after five looks is weak evidence. Reanalyse with maternal BMI continuous, checking the shape with a restricted cubic spline (3–4 knots at fixed centiles) and testing non-linearity by comparing spline and straight-line models; present the fitted curve with its CI band. Categories fixed in advance may be added as a description.

2. Adding three dummy variables for four categories to a trend model lowers SSE from 52.0 to 50.5. The category model has 120 residual df. Compute F for departure from a linear trend and say whether it suggests the trend model is inadequate (the 5% critical value of F on 3 and 120 df is 2.68).

F = [(52.0 − 50.5) ÷ 3] ÷ (50.5 ÷ 120) = 0.50 ÷ 0.421 = 1.19. This is below 2.68 (p > 0.05), so there is no evidence of departure from a straight-line trend; the one-coefficient trend model is the better summary. (No evidence of departure is not proof that the trend is exactly linear.)

1. One unusual point has an extreme predictor value but lies on the regression line; another has an ordinary predictor value but a very unexpected outcome. Which has high leverage, and which a large residual? Which is more likely to be influential?

The point with the extreme predictor value has high leverage (leverage depends only on x). The point with the ordinary x but unexpected outcome has a large residual. Neither is strongly influential on its own: the high-leverage point lies on the line, so removing it hardly changes the fit, and the large-residual point has little leverage to tilt the line (it mainly shifts the intercept slightly). Influence needs both at once, which Cook’s distance measures.

2. Why is an influential point a prompt to investigate rather than a reason to delete?

It may be a genuine observation showing real variation: deleting it discards information and makes the result look more certain than it is. Or it may be a data-entry error or a person outside the study population, who should be corrected or excluded. Only checking the record can tell which. Either way, report the fit with and without the point so readers can see how much the conclusion depends on it.

3. In a regression of 50 adults’ systolic BP on age, x̄ = 45 years and Sxx = 8,000 years². Compute the leverage of a 25-year-old and of a 75-year-old, and compare each with the average leverage.

h = 1/n + (x − x̄)²/Sxx. 25-year-old: 1/50 + (−20)²/8000 = 0.020 + 400/8000 = 0.020 + 0.050 = 0.070. 75-year-old: 0.020 + 30²/8000 = 0.020 + 900/8000 = 0.020 + 0.1125 = 0.1325. The average leverage is (k + 1)/n = 2/50 = 0.04, so the 25-year-old has 1.75 times and the 75-year-old 3.3 times the average. The 75-year-old could move the line most if their BP is far from its prediction.

1. In a two-predictor model, the adjusted coefficient for maternal education (years) on birthweight is 25 g per year, the coefficient for maternal height is 12 g per cm, and the slope of maternal height on education is 0.5 cm per year. What was the crude coefficient for education?

Crude slope = adjusted slope + (height coefficient) × (slope of height on education) = 25 + 12 × 0.5 = 25 + 6 = 31 g per year. About 6 g of the crude 31 g per year reflected the taller stature of more-educated mothers.

2. A colleague says “age is a confounder in every child-growth study”. Using the confounder and precision-covariate definitions, explain when age confounds a wealth–weight association and when it is only a precision covariate.

Age affects weight in every such study, and wealth cannot cause a child’s age, so age is never a mediator. But it confounds the wealth–weight association only if it is also associated with wealth in the population studied, for example if wealthier families bring older children to the clinic. Then the crude comparison mixes the wealth difference with an age difference, and adjustment moves the coefficient (as in §12.6: 0.90 → 0.62, with r = 0.16 between age and wealth). If age is unrelated to wealth (say, a sample with the same age distribution in every wealth group), it is only a precision covariate: adjusting leaves the wealth coefficient unchanged but shrinks its SE, because it removes age-driven variation from the residuals. Including it is worthwhile in both cases, but for different reasons.
